title: Memoize
description: Cache a pure function's results by argument key — repeated calls with the same input return the stored value without re-running the body. The optional keyFn lets callers serialize complex args.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: `memoize(fn)` returns a wrapped function such that calling the wrapper with arguments it's already seen returns the cached result without re-running `fn`. A few clarifying questions:"

• Purity — am I allowed to assume `fn` is pure? (Same args always yield same output, no side effects.)
• Cache key — what counts as 'same args'? Just primitives, or object arguments by content? Identity or structural comparison?
• Cache lifetime — does the cache live for the lifetime of the wrapper, or do I need eviction (LRU, TTL)?
• `this` binding — should the wrapper preserve `this` from the call site?
• Optional custom keyFn — should I accept one so the caller can override the default serialization?
sections.why: The purity question is the gating one — if `fn` reads `Date.now()` or mutates globals, memoizing it is incorrect, not just inefficient. Calling that out upfront signals you understand WHY caching works in the first place. The cache-lifetime question separates a toy implementation from a production one; for the interview, "lives as long as the wrapper" is almost always the right answer, but asking shows you've thought past the happy path.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the simplest version before generalizing.
sections.say:
"For a single-arg numeric function, the trivial version is `const cache = {}; const memoized = n => cache[n] !== undefined ? cache[n] : (cache[n] = fn(n))`. That works for `square(3)` repeatedly, but it has real limits:"

• Only one argument.
• Plain object keys collide on prototype names (`__proto__`).
• `cache[n] !== undefined` mis-classifies a legitimate cached `undefined` as a miss — would re-run `fn` forever for any function that returns `undefined`.

"To generalize: use a `Map` (handles any string key, no prototype collisions), use `cache.has(k)` instead of value comparison, and key by `JSON.stringify(args)` so any arg shape works."
sections.why: The 'cached undefined' bug is the senior-tier callout — most candidates write the `!== undefined` version and never notice it breaks for fns that legitimately return undefined. Naming it explicitly demonstrates that you understand caches need explicit presence checks (`has` / `in`), not value sentinels. The prototype-collision issue with plain objects is the other test — `Map` exists for exactly this reason.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.say:
"This is the classic cache-as-closure pattern. The wrapper closes over a private `Map` that lives as long as the wrapper does. Each call: compute a string key from the args (default: `JSON.stringify(args)`), check `cache.has(k)` — hit returns the stored value, miss runs `fn`, stores the result, and returns it."

"The closure topology is the load-bearing part: the cache is *captured*, not passed in, so it's private to this wrapper instance. Two separate `memoize(fn)` calls create two independent caches. That's why calling `memoize(fn)` and discarding the return value defeats the whole mechanism — the cache lives with the wrapper, not with `fn`."
sections.why: Naming both the closure capture AND the wrapper-instance-scoped lifetime is the distinguishing move. A candidate who says "I'd store results in a cache" without saying *where* the cache lives hasn't fully grasped the mechanism. Spelling out that two `memoize(fn)` calls produce two caches is the test — that's the difference between understanding closures and merely using them.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few call sequences to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three call sequences on `memoize(x => x * 2)`. The state to track per call: `cache` contents, the result returned, and how many times the underlying `fn` body actually ran."

examples.note: Mixed hits and misses — key '[3]' cached after first call, hit on positions 1 and 4.
examples.trace:
call #0 args=[3] → k='[3]' MISS → fn(3)=6, cache={'[3]':6}, bodyRuns=1
call #1 args=[3] → k='[3]' HIT  → return 6 (skip fn body)
call #2 args=[4] → k='[4]' MISS → fn(4)=8, cache={'[3]':6,'[4]':8}, bodyRuns=2
call #3 args=[5] → k='[5]' MISS → fn(5)=10, cache={'[3]':6,'[4]':8,'[5]':10}, bodyRuns=3
call #4 args=[3] → k='[3]' HIT  → return 6
→ results=[6,6,8,10,6], bodyRuns=3 (5 calls, 3 unique)

examples.note: All unique — every call misses, cache grows linearly, no hits.
examples.trace:
call #0 args=[1] → k='[1]' MISS → fn(1)=2, cache size 1
call #1 args=[2] → k='[2]' MISS → fn(2)=4, cache size 2
call #2 args=[3] → k='[3]' MISS → fn(3)=6, cache size 3
→ results=[2,4,6], bodyRuns=3 (worst case: memoize never helps)

examples.note: First miss, then two hits — the canonical 'amortize the work' case.
examples.trace:
call #0 args=[7] → k='[7]' MISS → fn(7)=14, cache={'[7]':14}, bodyRuns=1
call #1 args=[7] → k='[7]' HIT  → return 14
call #2 args=[7] → k='[7]' HIT  → return 14
→ results=[14,14,14], bodyRuns=1 (3 calls, 1 fn run — the whole point)

sections.why: Tracing the all-unique case is the move that surfaces the worst case — memoize doesn't help when there's no repetition, and the cache becomes pure overhead. Calling that out shows you understand the tradeoff. The mixed-hits-and-misses trace also exposes the key-collision risk: if `JSON.stringify` returned the same string for two different arg lists (which it doesn't for primitives, but does for non-stable object key ordering), the hits would return stale results.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Cached `undefined` — `cache.has(k)` is the correct guard, not `cache[k] !== undefined`. A function that returns `undefined` legitimately would otherwise re-run forever.
• Object arguments — `JSON.stringify({a:1, b:2})` and `JSON.stringify({b:2, a:1})` produce different strings even though the objects are structurally identical. Key ordering in literals is insertion-order in modern JS, but not guaranteed across constructors. Caller might need a custom keyFn.
• Cache eviction — no built-in eviction means a long-lived wrapper called with many distinct args grows unbounded. For production, wrap with an LRU (a `Map` plus delete-and-reinsert on hit gives you LRU semantics for free, since Map preserves insertion order).
• `this` binding — `fn(...args)` loses the call-site `this`. For method memoization, use `fn.apply(this, args)` instead.
• Non-serializable args (functions, Symbols, circular refs) — `JSON.stringify` drops them silently or throws on cycles. Custom keyFn needed.
• Async functions — memoize stores the returned Promise, so subsequent calls await the same in-flight Promise (de-duplication, not just caching). That's usually desirable, but worth noting.
• Rejected Promises — the cache stores the rejected Promise, so retries don't help. Often you want to delete on rejection.
sections.why: The cached-undefined and `cache.has` vs `cache[k] !== undefined` distinction is the single most common bug in this code. Calling it out unprompted shows you've debugged this before. The async/rejected-Promise edge is the modern-JS senior signal — most candidates think of memoize as a sync-only tool, and explicitly addressing how it interacts with Promises proves you've thought about real codebases that use it.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds, and what does this generalize to?
sections.say:
"Time per call is O(k) where k is the cost of computing the key (`JSON.stringify` cost), plus O(1) for the Map lookup, plus the original `fn` cost on a miss. For primitive args, the key cost is negligible. The whole point is that hits skip the `fn` body — for a fn that's expensive relative to the key serialization, the speedup is unbounded.

Space is O(unique-args-seen) — the cache grows to one entry per distinct key. For functions called with bounded input domains (a finite recursion, a fixed set of params), it's small. For functions called with unbounded input, you need eviction.

This is the canonical example of trading space for time via closure-state. The same pattern shows up in React's `useMemo` (cache by dep array), in dynamic programming top-down memoization (`fib(n)` with a cache flips O(2^n) to O(n)), and in HTTP request de-duplication (Promise cache keyed by URL). If you wanted me to extend: add LRU eviction with `maxSize`, or add TTL via timestamps in the cached value, or add weak-key support so object-keyed entries get GC'd when the key object dies."
sections.why: Naming the React `useMemo` and DP-memoization analogs is the transfer move — it proves you see memoize as a general technique with many surface forms, not a one-off interview snippet. The LRU/TTL/weak-key extensions show you've thought about how the toy version becomes a real one. The 'speedup is unbounded' phrasing is the right way to talk about the time bound: there's no clean O() number because it depends entirely on `fn`'s cost vs. the key cost.

walkthrough.intro: Step through memoize wrapping `x => x * 2`. The trace feeds a sequence of single-arg calls; the cache state and `results` array (one per call) evolve in the state panel. Repeated args hit the cache and skip the body entirely — that's the whole point.

examples.label: calls=[3,3,4,5,3] — hits at positions 1, 4 (key '[3]' cached after first call)
calls=[1,2,3] — all unique, every call misses + populates
calls=[7,7,7] — first miss, then two hits in a row

trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter memoize(fn) — fn is x => x*2; call sequence=${JSON.stringify(calls)}`, state: { calls, bodyRuns } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'init cache (empty Map)', state: { calls, cache: [], bodyRuns } };
yield { line: 5, label: 'no keyFn provided — default toKey = JSON.stringify(args)', state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns } };
yield { line: 6, label: `call #${i}: wrapped(${args.join(', ')})`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args } };
yield { line: 7, label: `compute key = JSON.stringify(args) = '${k}'`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args, k } };
yield { line: 9, label: `HIT — cache.get('${k}') = ${hit}; skip fn body entirely`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args, k, hit } };
yield { line: 9, label: `MISS — '${k}' not in cache; run fn(...args)`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args, k } };
yield { line: 10, label: `fn(${args.join(', ')}) → ${v} (bodyRuns now ${bodyRuns})`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args, k, v } };
yield { line: 11, label: `cache.set('${k}', ${v}) — store for next call`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], i, args, k, v } };

yield { line: 13, label: `done — bodyRuns=${bodyRuns}, results=${JSON.stringify(results)}`, state: { calls, cache: [...cache.entries()], bodyRuns, results: [...results], returns: JSON.stringify(results) } };

notes: Default key is JSON.stringify(args) — fast and good enough for primitives + plain objects, but won't distinguish two objects with identical content from one passed twice.
Memoization only works for pure fns. A fn that reads `Date.now()` or mutates globals will return stale results on cache hits.
Use Map (not a plain object) for keys — Map handles any string cleanly and avoids prototype-pollution edge cases like `__proto__`.

questions.q: Calling a memoized fn with the same args three times calls the underlying fn how many times?
options: 3 — memoize records calls but still invokes the body each time
0 — the wrapper short-circuits before reaching the underlying fn even on the first call
2 — the cache stores at most one value, so every other call has to recompute

questions.q: Why is the default key `JSON.stringify(args)` insufficient for some inputs?
options: `JSON.stringify` on an args array always returns `'[]'` because rest-parameter arrays aren't iterable in serialization
Functions, undefined, Symbols, and circular refs don't serialize cleanly — also two distinct objects with the same shape collide
Each call to `JSON.stringify` allocates a new string identity, so cache keys never compare equal across calls
`JSON.stringify` strips numeric precision past 6 digits, so two close-but-distinct numeric args collapse to one cache entry
Whenever the function takes more than one argument — the default key only captures the first
When the function isn't pure — same args may legitimately need different outputs
When the function returns an object — Map values must be primitives to be cached
When the wrapped function is recursive — the cache breaks the base-case detection

questions.q: What benefit does an explicit keyFn provide over the default?
options: Avoids the cost of JSON.stringify and lets you collapse equivalent-but-not-identical inputs to one key
It tracks the key insertion order so the cache can be replayed in call order during hot-reload
It lets the cache hold non-string keys directly (Map can otherwise only store stringified keys)
It enables async support — the default keyFn does not await Promise-typed arguments

exercises.prompt: Fill in the memoize so the call counter only increments once per unique input.

blanks.hint: fetch the stored value by key

L3.prompt: Implement memoize(fn, keyFn?). Call a counter-tracking slow fn with two repeated and one unique arg; show results and that the underlying fn ran only twice.
hints: Use a Map keyed by JSON.stringify(args) when no keyFn is provided.
Check cache.has(k) before computing — the whole point is to skip fn() on hits.
Accept an optional keyFn for callers who need custom serialization.
